title: Trump and Vance berate Zelensky, defend Putin, and threaten to end Ukraine
description_short: Trump and Vance berate Zelensky, defend Putin, and threaten to end Ukraine

description_long:
Donald Trump and J.D. Vance confronted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a White House meeting on February 28, 2025. Discussion of a ceasefire and a proposed minerals agreement turned into an argument over diplomacy, gratitude and Ukraine's security. The meeting ended early without a signed agreement, while reporting raised the possibility that Washington would withhold further military assistance.

Zelensky emphasized that an agreement with Russia needed credible guarantees, pointing to earlier commitments that had not prevented renewed war. Vance responded by accusing him of disrespect toward the administration and challenging his approach in front of reporters. Trump warned that Ukraine was risking a wider war and pressed Zelensky to change his position. The disagreement therefore concerned both the terms of a potential settlement and the public treatment of an allied leader whose country was fighting Russia's invasion. Reports described consideration of interrupting a shipment of military equipment after the meeting; the discussion did not amount to a completed termination of all American support. The confrontation exposed a substantial diplomatic rupture at a moment when Ukraine sought reassurance about future assistance.

The proclamation commuted the sentences of fourteen named people, pardoned other convicted defendants and directed dismissal of pending indictments. It affected prosecutions arising from the Capitol attack, including cases involving violence against police and organized efforts to obstruct the transfer of presidential power. description_long: Donald Trump pardoned former Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio in August 2017 after his criminal-contempt conviction for defying a federal court order concerning discriminatory immigration enforcement. The pardon came before sentencing and outside the usual Justice Department review process. It drew criticism over respect for judicial authority and the protection of a political ally. The underlying contempt case concerned failure to obey an order restricting practices that targeted Latino residents. title: Trump: Federal judge rules against ‘DOGE' in its attempts to seize USIP
description_short: Trump: Federal judge rules against ‘DOGE' in its attempts to seize USIP
description_medium: A federal judge ruled that the Trump administration unlawfully removed the United States Institute of Peace’s board and declared the administration’s replacement appointments void. The case challenged efforts by DOGE and other officials to take control of the institute and its Washington headquarters. The ruling addressed authority over the organization; later appeals and the institute’s operational status were separate questions.
description_long: In February 2025, Donald Trump issued an executive order declaring the United States Institute of Peace unnecessary and demanding its closure. The institute said it was independent of the executive branch. The next month, Trump fired its board, and DOGE affiliates forcibly removed board members and staff. A U.S. district court judge, Beryl Howell, ruled for the former board and staff, finding the removals unlawful. Howell also declared null and void the administration's claim to USIP's Washington headquarters, reported as a $500 million property. Court filings say DOGE representatives accompanied by FBI agents had earlier tried to enter the headquarters and were turned away. The defendants included Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the U.S. DOGE Service, and other officials and agencies. The ruling addressed control of the institute and its property; subsequent appeals and the institute’s final operational status remained separate questions.
